questions.title: Exceptions practice 1
choices: NumberFormatException
ClassCastException
IOException
NullPointerException
questions.explanation: The text does not match Java's integer format. The method reports that content problem with NumberFormatException.

questions.title: Exceptions practice 2
questions.code: String load(Path path) { /* reads a file */ }
questions.prompt: What must a method do with a checked IOException?
choices: Catch it or declare it with `throws`
Ignore it because all exceptions are optional
Convert it to an int
Place it in a static field
questions.explanation: Java's compiler tracks checked exceptions. The method must handle the IOException or state in its signature that a caller is responsible for it.

questions.title: Trace Exceptions
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
accepted: Credits must be a whole number
questions.explanation: The catch type matches the conversion failure. Code after the failed parse inside try is skipped, then execution continues after catch. The resulting output is 'Credits must be a whole number'.

questions.title: Exceptions practice 5
questions.prompt: Why catch `NumberFormatException` here instead of the broad `Exception`?
choices: So an unrelated bug like a NullPointerException is not mislabeled as "Bad number"
Because Exception cannot be caught in Java
Because a narrow catch runs faster
Because NumberFormatException must always be caught to compile
questions.explanation: The message claims the input was a bad number, so the catch should match only that case. Catching `Exception` would also swallow a NullPointerException or a logic bug and print the same misleading message. It is about honesty of the handler, not speed; `NumberFormatException` is unchecked, so nothing forces you to catch it.

questions.title: Exceptions concept check 1
questions.prompt: When Java code wraps one exception in another, what should it preserve?
choices: If you create a new exception, pass the original one as its cause. Without that link, the stack trace loses the failure that started the chain and makes diagnosis harder.
Catch every exception and continue without evidence.
Use exceptions for ordinary choices an if statement can handle.
Replace the original error with a vague one and drop the cause.
questions.explanation: If you create a new exception, pass the original one as its cause. Without that link, the stack trace loses the failure that started the chain and makes diagnosis harder. This matters because exception code should handle failures at a layer that can respond without hiding unrelated programming mistakes.

questions.title: Exceptions concept check 2
questions.prompt: Which choice describes a reliable Exceptions practice?
choices: Wrap a whole program in one broad protected block.
Catch a type that matches the recovery you can perform.
Catch errors at a layer that cannot recover.
Hide unexpected programming mistakes.
questions.explanation: Catch a type that matches the recovery you can perform. This matters because exception code should handle failures at a layer that can respond without hiding unrelated programming mistakes.

questions.title: Exceptions concept check 3
questions.prompt: Which Exceptions code review note is accurate?
choices: Raise an exception after the function already returned successfully.
Use an exception to skip normal loop logic.
Keep the protected block small.
Report failure without enough context to debug it.
questions.explanation: Keep the protected block small. This matters because exception code should handle failures at a layer that can respond without hiding unrelated programming mistakes.

questions.title: Exceptions concept check 4
questions.prompt: Which Exceptions habit prevents a common mistake?
choices: Ignore cleanup around code that can fail.
Catch a base exception type when a specific one is known.
Turn every invalid input into the same generic message.
Distinguish checked exceptions from runtime exceptions.
questions.explanation: Distinguish checked exceptions from runtime exceptions. This matters because exception code should handle failures at a layer that can respond without hiding unrelated programming mistakes.

questions.title: Exceptions concept check 5
choices: Preserve an original cause when wrapping.
Keep running after required work did not happen.
Handle errors by returning unrelated default data.
Assume the absence of a crash proves the operation succeeded.
questions.explanation: Preserve an original cause when wrapping. This matters because exception code should handle failures at a layer that can respond without hiding unrelated programming mistakes.

questions.title: Exceptions concept check 6
choices: Use try/catch around code that cannot throw.
Use try-with-resources for closeable objects.
Make callers guess whether a failure happened.
Discard stack-trace information during wrapping.
questions.explanation: Use try-with-resources for closeable objects. This matters because exception code should handle failures at a layer that can respond without hiding unrelated programming mistakes.
